title: Process Handle Leak Detection
exclusions: Detects a policy-defined pattern of sustained growth in the Windows `Process\Handle Count` gauge for one continuously observed host, performance-counter instance, and process ID. It does not prove that handles are leaked, identify handle types or creation stacks, establish a universal safe handle count, calculate system-wide handle capacity, or diagnose kernel pool exhaustion. It excludes `_Total`, `Idle`, PID 0, process lifetimes shorter than six complete five-minute buckets, buckets with fewer than four samples of either required counter, and any PID change inside a bucket. The base rule requires six complete buckets, at least four of five bucket-to-bucket increases, a latest average of at least 5,000 handles, a net increase of at least 1,000 handles, and at least 25% growth. Those are explicit starting policy values, not Microsoft limits. Missing, delayed, duplicated, localized, multikv-shaped, nonnumeric, or identity-ambiguous telemetry is source failure rather than healthy process behavior. No exception lookup is applied by the base SPL, and this operational use case makes no security, malicious-intent, remediation, or regulatory-attestation claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_process_handle_growth` saved-search definition, ACL, fixed time bounds, schedule, dispatch and triggered-alert history; effective `[perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth]` configuration and `btool` output; Windows, add-on, forwarder, and search-platform versions; expected-host inventory and source-health results; and each result row containing host, performance-counter instance, PID, observation bounds, complete bucket and rising-transition counts, first/latest/minimum/peak averages, net increase, and percentage increase. Preserve the corresponding raw `Handle Count` and `ID Process` events, same-time Windows Performance Monitor or `Get-Counter` samples, Process Explorer or approved debugger evidence used for diagnosis, process lifecycle/change context, bounded notification exception, incident disposition, and dated positive/negative control outputs. These artifacts show that received counter samples met the documented candidate rule; they do not prove a leak, handle type, allocation call stack, root cause, remediation, or complete fleet coverage. This documentation-only review created no runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated event index with fixed absolute bounds covering exactly six completed five-minute buckets, ingest one event per minute for `counter="Handle Count"` and one for `counter="ID Process"`, all with `host=win-handle-positive`, `object=Process`, `instance=worker`, and PID 4242. Set the six bucket-average handle counts to 4000, 4300, 4700, 5100, 5400, and 5600, with five samples per counter per bucket. Point a copy of the SPL at that index and fixed window. Expect exactly one row with `complete_buckets=6`, `rising_transitions=5`, `first_avg_handles=4000`, `latest_avg_handles=5600`, `handle_increase=1600`, and `handle_increase_pct=40`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated fixed-time variants and expect zero candidate rows for each: latest average 4,999; net increase 999; growth 24.99%; only three rising transitions; only five complete buckets; fewer than four `Handle Count` or `ID Process` samples in one bucket; PID changes from 4242 to 5252 inside a bucket; PID 0; negative or nonnumeric values; a process restart that reuses `instance=worker` under a new PID; localized counter names; multikv events without the documented scalar fields; and samples outside the delayed window. Verify a separate source-health search reports incomplete, stale, duplicated, localized, malformed, and identity-ambiguous inputs instead of treating their zero primary rows as healthy.

dataSources: Primary source: local Windows Performance Data Helper counters collected through a custom `[perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth]` input by the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), in `mode=single`, routed by local convention to `index=perfmon sourcetype=Perfmon:Process` every 60 seconds. Required `Process` counters are `Handle Count` (unitless count of handles currently open by the process; a last-observed gauge, not a rate or cumulative total) and `ID Process` (decimal process identifier used to reject instance reuse). Splunk metadata and event fields required by the SPL are `_time`, `host`, `object`, `counter`, `instance`, and numeric `Value`. `useEnglishOnly=true` stabilizes exact English object and counter names. The index is configurable but must match the search.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for supported local Windows `perfmon://` collection and search-time knowledge. Deploy the collection stanza to Windows Universal Forwarders or full Splunk Enterprise instances and the add-on knowledge to the tiers required by the topology. A Universal Forwarder executes the local input; it is not Splunkbase app 617 and is not a substitute for the add-on.
spl:
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Process" object="Process" counter IN ("Handle Count","ID Process") instance!="_Total" instance!="Idle" earliest=-35m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval handle_count_sample=if(counter=="Handle Count",tonumber(Value),null()), process_id_sample=if(counter=="ID Process",tonumber(Value),null())
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(handle_count_sample) as bucket_handle_count max(handle_count_sample) as bucket_peak_handle_count latest(process_id_sample) as process_id dc(process_id_sample) as process_ids count(handle_count_sample) as handle_samples count(process_id_sample) as pid_samples by _time host instance
| where handle_samples>=4 AND pid_samples>=4 AND process_ids=1 AND process_id>0 AND bucket_handle_count>=0 AND bucket_peak_handle_count>=0
| eval process_id=round(process_id,0), bucket_handle_count=round(bucket_handle_count,2), bucket_peak_handle_count=round(bucket_peak_handle_count,0)
| sort 0 host instance process_id _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(bucket_handle_count) as previous_bucket_handle_count by host instance process_id
| eval rising_transition=if(isnull(previous_bucket_handle_count),null(),if(bucket_handle_count>previous_bucket_handle_count,1,0))
| stats count as complete_buckets sum(rising_transition) as rising_transitions min(_time) as observation_start max(_time) as last_bucket_start earliest(bucket_handle_count) as first_avg_handles latest(bucket_handle_count) as latest_avg_handles min(bucket_handle_count) as minimum_avg_handles max(bucket_peak_handle_count) as peak_sample_handles by host instance process_id
| eval observation_end=last_bucket_start+300, handle_increase=latest_avg_handles-first_avg_handles, handle_increase_pct=if(first_avg_handles>0,100*handle_increase/first_avg_handles,null())
| where complete_buckets=6 AND rising_transitions>=4 AND latest_avg_handles>=5000 AND handle_increase>=1000 AND handle_increase_pct>=25
| eval first_avg_handles=round(first_avg_handles,2), latest_avg_handles=round(latest_avg_handles,2), minimum_avg_handles=round(minimum_avg_handles,2), handle_increase=round(handle_increase,2), handle_increase_pct=round(handle_increase_pct,2), severity="high", use_case="UC-1.2.22"
| table observation_start observation_end host instance process_id severity complete_buckets rising_transitions first_avg_handles latest_avg_handles minimum_avg_handles peak_sample_handles handle_increase handle_increase_pct use_case
| sort 0 -handle_increase_pct -latest_avg_handles host instance process_id
description: Identifies a suspected Windows process handle leak by following the same process ID and performance-counter instance across six complete five-minute buckets. It requires mostly monotonic growth plus absolute-count, net-growth, and percentage-growth policy gates, while rejecting sparse samples and process identity changes. The result is a triage candidate; only handle-level diagnostics can confirm a leak.
value: An unchecked handle leak can gradually consume object and pool resources, destabilize a service, and force an emergency restart even when CPU and ordinary memory charts look acceptable. A persistent, identity-aware trend can prevent that disruption by giving Windows and application owners time to preserve diagnostic state, locate the leaking handle type and allocation path, and correct the software before availability is affected, without paging on every short-lived handle burst.
implementation: Install `Splunk_TA_windows`, deploy one explicit local `[perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth]` stanza for `Handle Count` and `ID Process` with all instances, `mode=single`, `useEnglishOnly=true`, `interval=60`, and `index=perfmon`, then qualify field shape, units, cadence, duplicate stanzas, and process identity. Save the SPL as `windows_process_handle_growth` and schedule it every five minutes; it evaluates six completed buckets after a five-minute indexing delay. Treat findings as suspected leaks and confirm with Process Explorer, Handle, Application Verifier, or WinDbg under an approved diagnostic procedure.
visualization: Put source health first: expected hosts without both counters, newest-event age, per-counter sample counts, duplicate-stanza indicators, and scalar-field/mode failures. For qualified candidates, use a 24-hour line chart of five-minute average `Handle Count` by `host`, `instance`, and `process_id`, with the 5,000 policy line and process start/restart annotations; display handles as counts, never percentages. Add a ranked table matching the alert columns and drilldowns to the two raw counter series, Process Explorer evidence, service lifecycle, process private bytes, and system paged/nonpaged pool. Show telemetry gaps as unknown, and label the panel “suspected sustained handle growth,” not “confirmed leak.”
schema: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Perfmon event fields plus Windows Process performance-counter semantics; partial CIM Endpoint.Processes context
dataModelAcceleration: The Endpoint.Processes dataset can normalize process identity and lifecycle context, but it does not preserve the raw Windows `Handle Count`, `ID Process` pairing, performance-counter instance, per-counter sample completeness, six-bucket persistence, or growth gates required by this use case. No semantically equivalent `cimSpl` or accelerated `tstats` alert is claimed. At fleet scale, use a purpose-built summary only if it retains the native handle count and unit, PID, instance, host/time identity, sample counts, and bucket validity.

knownFalsePositives:
The search reports a sustained measurement pattern, not a proven leak. A process can legitimately retain handles while useful state grows.

1. **IIS or application-server warm-up** — `w3wp`, Java, .NET, database, and similar workers can open files, registry keys, events, sockets, or synchronization objects while loading applications, pools, caches, or tenants. Compare against process start time, deployment/change records, request volume, and the documented steady-state plateau. Growth that stops and later releases is not the same as an unbounded leak.

2. **Approved load, soak, failover, or scale test** — A test can deliberately increase concurrent sessions and their handles for longer than 30 minutes. Confirm the exact host, PID, test owner, approved UTC interval, expected concurrency curve, and recovery criteria. Preserve the result as evidence and suppress only notification during the bounded test.

3. **Backup, antivirus, indexing, or file-crawl worker** — Microsoft Defender, backup agents, search indexers, and inventory scanners can hold many file or registry handles while traversing a large working set. Correlate the process identity, job schedule, scanned-object count, and Process Explorer handle types. Continued growth after the job ends remains actionable.

4. **Connection, queue, or tenant population growth** — A broker, proxy, service host, or management agent can retain one or more handles per active connection, queue, object, or managed tenant. Compare handle growth with the application's own concurrency and object-count metrics. If the ratio is stable and both decline together, tune policy for that service rather than declaring a leak.

5. **Process startup or rolling deployment** — The same `instance` label can be reused when a worker exits and another starts. The SPL groups by `ID Process` and rejects PID changes inside a bucket, but it cannot prove executable path, service identity, or boot-unique process identity from these two counters. Check start time and deployment state before joining findings across separate dispatches.

6. **Performance-counter instance renumbering** — Concurrent processes with the same image name can receive labels such as `worker`, `worker#1`, and `worker#2`; labels may be reassigned as processes exit. `ID Process` is therefore mandatory. If labels move between PIDs, use raw samples and process inventory to follow the PID; do not suppress all instances sharing the base label.

7. **Bursting handles around scheduled work** — Certificate rotation, log rollover, plug-in discovery, report generation, or batch import can produce mostly rising buckets and exceed all starting gates before releasing handles. Check whether the count returns toward its pre-job level after the documented window and whether new handles are balanced by closes in Process Explorer or tracing.

8. **Duplicate collection or replayed events** — Two enabled perfmon stanzas, deployment-server plus local configuration, or queue replay can satisfy sample-count gates and distort bucket averages. Compare expected 60-second cadence, `_indextime`, effective `btool` precedence, raw event multiplicity, and forwarder identity. Repair collection rather than deduplicating measurements with unknown provenance.

9. **Threshold mismatch across process roles** — Five thousand handles, 1,000 net handles, 25%, four rises, and 30 minutes are catalogue starting policy, not Windows limits. A stable high-scale service may safely exceed 5,000, while a lower-count process can leak slowly below every gate. Establish per-service baselines and separate warning policies without claiming that a tuned number proves safety.

10. **Counter localization or event-shape drift** — Without `useEnglishOnly=true`, translated names will not match. `PerfmonMk:Process` multikv events do not necessarily expose the documented one-counter scalar `Value` contract. Missing rows are collection failure, not suppression or health; qualify and version any alternate normalization separately.

**Safe suppression:** keep the base search and source-health controls unchanged. If notification suppression is approved, apply a separate `windows_process_handle_exceptions.csv` lookup after the final result, keyed by exact `host`, `instance`, `process_id`, and `policy_id`, with numeric `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, image-name-only entries, open-ended records, and exceptions for missing or malformed telemetry. Retain suppressed findings and review expiration.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Windows process-resource trend; no adversary behavior or intent is asserted)

cost.search_load_notes: At a 60-second interval in single-event mode, two counters produce 2,880 events per process instance per day: about 576,000 events per 200-process host before metadata and indexing overhead. The five-minute search scans a delayed 30-minute window and groups by host, instance, PID, and bucket without joins or subsearches. Canary-measure actual process cardinality, bytes, and dispatch cost.
sources: Windows Process Handle Count and ID Process counters
Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows perfmon input

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement contract

Assign a Windows platform owner, Splunk collection owner, search-content owner, and application/service escalation path. Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) on the Windows collection tier and make its parsing and search-time knowledge available wherever the topology requires it. A Universal Forwarder or full Splunk Enterprise instance must be able to enumerate local Windows performance counters and send them to an approved event index. The search role needs index access and permission to save and schedule a search; diagnostic tooling and alert-action identities must be separately governed. No domain administrator, remote WMI, process-termination, debugger, or service-restart privilege is required for this read-only counter collection.

`Process\Handle Count` is a unitless **current count** of handles open by a process, summed across its threads. It is a gauge: the latest observation is the current count, not handles opened per second and not a cumulative lifetime total. A rising line is evidence for investigation, not proof of a leak. Legitimate work can retain handles, and a leaking process can remain below any fixed count. Microsoft provides no universal 5,000-handle failure boundary. This rule's latest count of 5,000, net increase of 1,000, 25% increase, and four of five rising transitions are starting triage policy values that must be baselined by process role.

`Process\ID Process` is collected with `Handle Count` because the `instance` string is not a durable process identity. Multiple processes with the same image name can be exposed as a base instance and numbered instances; labels can be reused as processes exit. The SPL requires one nonzero PID in each bucket and groups the trend by host, instance, and PID. This blocks obvious restarts and reassignment but still does not provide executable path, service name, command line, start time, boot ID, or a globally unique process identity. Use approved process inventory or incident diagnostics for those facts.

The temporal contract is explicit. With `interval=60`, each five-minute bucket should contain about five values for each counter. A bucket qualifies with at least four samples of both counters, one PID, nonnegative handle values, and PID greater than zero. The search evaluates six completed buckets from 35 minutes ago up to five minutes ago, leaving the newest five minutes for indexing. It requires at least four of the five transitions to rise, then applies all three magnitude gates. One flat or falling transition is tolerated; two are not. Missing or malformed samples fail closed and belong in source health. Change interval, sample minimum, delay, persistence, or thresholds only through a versioned policy and rerun all controls.

## Step 1 — Configure the supported Process counter input

Do not edit the add-on's `default` directory. Deploy a version-controlled local configuration such as `%SPLUNK_HOME%\etc\apps\Splunk_TA_windows\local\inputs.conf` through the approved deployment mechanism:

```ini
[perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth]
disabled = 0
object = Process
counters = Handle Count; ID Process
instances = *
interval = 60
mode = single
useEnglishOnly = true
index = perfmon
sourcetype = Perfmon:Process
```

The custom stanza name prevents this narrow contract from being confused with a broad default Process input. `instances=*` is required because the object is per process. `mode=single` is the event shape assumed by the SPL: scalar `object`, `counter`, `instance`, and `Value` fields. Keep this event-index feed separate from `PerfmonMk:Process` multikv events and `PerfmonMetrics:Process` metric-index data; each requires different normalization or `mstats`. `useEnglishOnly=true` invokes English counter names and requires explicit English object/counter text.

Before fleet rollout, inspect the effective stanza on canaries:

```powershell
& "$env:SPLUNK_HOME\bin\splunk.exe" btool inputs list perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth --debug
Get-Counter '\Process(*)\Handle Count','\Process(*)\ID Process' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 3
```

Confirm one winning stanza, the intended local app path, enabled state, 60-second interval, event index, single mode, source type, English names, and all instances. Verify system time, stable Splunk `host`, output queues, and target-index permissions. Process cardinality drives volume: two counters at one-minute cadence create 2,880 events per process instance per day, or roughly 576,000 for a host averaging 200 instances. Measure event bytes, host cardinality, forwarder CPU, and indexing/search cost on representative canaries before deployment. If this volume is unacceptable, use a longer tested interval or a purpose-built collector/summary; do not silently sample only selected image names and claim fleet coverage.

## Step 2 — Validate ingestion, field shape, identity, and source health

Run a 30-minute qualification search:

```spl
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Process" object="Process" counter IN ("Handle Count","ID Process") earliest=-30m
| eval numeric_value=tonumber(Value)
| stats count min(numeric_value) as minimum max(numeric_value) as maximum latest(_time) as newest dc(counter) as counters by host instance counter
| eval age_seconds=now()-newest
| sort 0 host instance counter
```

Each live instance should have both counter rows, numeric nonnegative values, roughly 30 observations per counter, and a newest event within two intervals plus measured indexing delay. `ID Process` should be an integer and greater than zero except special instances that the primary search excludes. Inspect raw events to confirm one scalar counter/value pair per event and that `_time` represents collection time. Compare same-time samples with Windows **Performance Monitor > Monitoring Tools > Performance Monitor** after adding `Process(*)\Handle Count` and `Process(*)\ID Process`, or use `Get-Counter`. Sampling times can differ slightly; instance/PID pairing and order of magnitude must agree.

Build a source-health search independent of the detection. Maintain expected-host inventory and report: no Process events; stale newest event; missing one required counter; localized or misspelled names; `PerfmonMk:Process`/multikv shape; nonnumeric, negative, or fractional PID; PID 0 outside expected special instances; two PIDs inside one host/instance/bucket; fewer or substantially more samples than cadence predicts; duplicated effective stanzas; forwarder queue delay; index/source-type drift; host identity collision; and collection volume above approved limits. Do not use `fillnull value=0`: zero handles or PID has semantic meaning, and fabricated values can hide identity failure. A silent candidate search is never proof that collection is healthy.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the sustained-growth search

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_process_handle_growth`, schedule it every five minutes on a five-minute boundary, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. Keep `earliest=-35m@m latest=-5m@m` in the SPL or move equivalent fixed bounds to saved-search configuration, but do not set conflicting windows in both places. The five-minute delay must exceed measured p95 ingestion latency; delayed data belongs in source health, not an automatically expanding alert window.

The base search selects the exact index, source type, object, counters, and non-special instances. The first `eval` converts `Value` into one unit-specific handle field and one identity field. `bin` creates six five-minute buckets. `stats` calculates the average and peak handle count, obtains the latest PID, counts distinct PIDs, and counts nonnull samples for each counter. The validity gate keeps only sufficiently sampled buckets with one positive PID and nonnegative handle values.

After deterministic sorting, `streamstats current=f window=1` supplies the immediately preceding bucket average for the same host, instance, and PID. `rising_transition` is one only when the current average is greater. The final aggregation counts six buckets and up to five transitions, preserves observation bounds and first/latest/minimum/peak values, and derives net and percentage growth. The alert uses `AND`: six buckets, at least four rises, latest average at least 5,000, increase at least 1,000, and increase at least 25%. A candidate can meet one or several conditions without alerting. The output deliberately says `instance`, not executable path, and PID is retained as a number.

This is a lagging trend control. It can miss a rapid leak that crashes in under 30 minutes and a slow leak below the magnitude gates. Pair it with service-failure, application-error, system pool, and source-health monitoring. Tune a separate policy per process role when evidence justifies it. Do not replace the rule with a 24-row moving average unless the process identity and restart boundary remain explicit; PID reuse over long windows makes naive baselines unsafe.

## Step 4 — Test logic, identity boundaries, and native truth

Use an isolated event index and absolute fixture timestamps. Load the positive scenario's 60 events: two counters, five one-minute observations, six buckets. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds. Assert one exact row and verify each intermediate bucket has five samples, one PID, the expected average, and the expected transition. Confirm the observation end is five minutes after the sixth bucket start.

Run each negative independently. Exercise exact boundaries: latest 5,000 qualifies and 4,999.99 does not; net 1,000 qualifies and 999.99 does not; 25% qualifies and 24.99% does not; four rises qualify and three do not; four samples per counter qualify and three do not. Confirm a PID change in a bucket, a new PID after restart, PID 0, localized names, nonnumeric values, a seventh out-of-window bucket, and incomplete data produce no candidate. Source health must report every telemetry-invalid variant.

On a Windows canary, compare indexed and native counter values during ordinary startup, normal load, a planned workload increase, and process restart. A synthetic fixture proves SPL arithmetic; a canary proves collection shape and units; neither proves a software leak or production threshold. Do not create a leak, exhaust handles, enable invasive tracing, attach a debugger, or restart a production service merely to fire the rule. Record tester, dates, exact bounds, Windows/add-on/forwarder/search-platform versions, fixture checksum, expected and actual rows, alert delivery, native comparison, workload owner, and exception behavior. Keep `status=draft` until runtime and service-owner acceptance is complete.

## Step 5 — Operationalize triage, dashboards, and evidence

Use the unit-labelled dashboard in `visualization`, with source health above candidate trends. When a finding arrives, first confirm six buckets, both counter sample counts, one PID, current source health, no duplicated stanza, stable host identity, and process lifecycle. Compare current native Handle Count and PID. In Process Explorer, select the identified process and use handle view to examine objects opened and closed; the utility can show open handles, but a point-in-time list still does not prove which creation path failed to close them. The command-line Sysinternals Handle utility can supply a controlled snapshot where approved.

Correlate the trend with process start time, service/deployment/failover records, request/session/queue counts, scheduled backup or scanning jobs, process private bytes/working set, and system paged/nonpaged pool. If handles rise with a bounded workload and return afterward, document the expected behavior. If they continue rising after work stabilizes, engage the software owner and preserve diagnostics before restart. Application Verifier handle checks and WinDbg `!htrace` can record creation/close stacks, but they change diagnostic overhead and require expert approval and a safe environment. Prefer reproduction in a test environment.

Do not automatically terminate the PID, restart the service, recycle an application pool, attach a debugger, or deploy tracing from this alert. PID reuse can target the wrong process, and restart destroys the state needed to diagnose a leak. Follow the service runbook, verify current identity independently, preserve before-state evidence, obtain change approval, and validate both handle recovery and service health afterward. Retain the artifacts named in `evidence`; the 30-day warm-retention estimate is not a mandate.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot without converting unknowns into health

- **No `Perfmon:Process` events:** verify add-on assignment, `disabled=0`, effective `btool` stanza, Windows service, index/routing, output queues, and role access. Inspect `splunkd.log` for the exact `perfmon://ProcessHandleGrowth` input; do not substitute unrelated WMI process snapshots and claim equivalent cadence or fields.
- **Counter names are missing or translated:** confirm `useEnglishOnly=true`, explicit English names, and native availability with `Get-Counter -ListSet Process` or `typeperf -qx`. Repair configuration instead of adding guessed translations to SPL.
- **Events use `PerfmonMk:Process`:** collection is multikv and does not satisfy the scalar `counter`/`Value` contract. Restore `mode=single` or create and test a separate normalization with cardinality controls.
- **Events are in a metric index:** author an `mstats` implementation against verified metric names and dimensions. An event-index search cannot query metric data, and switching storage does not preserve field names automatically.
- **Sample count is too high:** look for two enabled Process stanzas, deployment/local precedence, replay, or an interval shorter than 60 seconds. Do not accept duplicates merely because averages look plausible.
- **One instance has several PIDs:** a process exited/restarted or duplicate-name labels were reassigned within the bucket. Keep the identity gate, inspect raw chronology, and use process start-time inventory if the service needs faster detection.
- **The process leaks but no alert appears:** it may crash before 30 minutes, grow below 5,000, add fewer than 1,000 handles, rise less than 25%, oscillate, or change PID/instance. That is expected scope, not a reason to relabel the result. Build a separately tested policy for that process.
- **A high stable process does not alert:** expected. This search detects growth, not a universal maximum. Review the ranked dashboard and service baseline; do not remove persistence just to page on a large but stable count.
- **A candidate later falls:** investigate bounded work, cleanup cadence, delayed closes, and fixture/source duplication. The alert truth is the documented historical window; recovery changes response priority but does not make the prior measurements false.
- **CIM/tstats cannot reproduce the finding:** expected. Endpoint process normalization does not preserve this complete native counter and persistence contract. Keep the raw-event search or build a purpose-specific governed summary.
grandmaExplanation: We watch whether one Windows program keeps collecting more open connections to system objects without settling back down. If that growth lasts long enough and becomes large enough, we ask the team to investigate before the program becomes unstable.
